core_principles: The forward lunge is a closed kinetic chain exercise used for lower body strengthening and rehabilitation.
During the forward lunge, the quadriceps (rectus femoris) and gastrocnemius undergo eccentric contractions.
The hamstrings do not contract eccentrically during the forward lunge; instead, they perform isometric contractions during the first part of the stance phase.
Coaches and athletes should not rely on the forward lunge for eccentric hamstring strengthening, despite common beliefs.
common_mistakes: Prescribing or performing the forward lunge under the false assumption that it provides eccentric strengthening for the hamstring muscle group.
specific_findings: Five experienced athletes performed ﬁve cycles for each of the walking and jumping forward lunges.
No hamstring eccentric contractions were found; however, the hamstrings showed isometric contractions during the ﬁrst part of the stance phase.
Eccentric contractions in both the quadriceps and gastrocnemius were observed during the lunge.

core_principles: The walking forward lunge (WFL) and jumping forward lunge (JFL) utilize different upper body and hip angles.
During the jumping forward lunge, the hip and upper body lean more forward compared to the walking forward lunge.
Both lunge variations involve eccentric and concentric actions of the quadriceps, hamstrings, and gastrocnemius muscles.
specific_findings: The study analyzed five experienced male athletes with a mean age of 31 (range 27–39) years.
EMG was recorded at 1000 Hz with a frequency bandwidth of 16–500 Hz and a common mode rejection ratio of 114 dB.
Lateral hamstrings electrodes were placed 50% on the line between the ischial tuberosity and the lateral epicondyle of the tibia.
Rectus femoris electrodes were placed 50% on the line from the anterior spina iliaca superior to the superior part of the patella.
Lateral gastrocnemius electrodes were placed at the proximal 1/3 of the line between the head of fibula and the heel.

core_principles: Jumping forward lunges (JFL) elicit higher muscle activation (EMG) in the rectus femoris, lateral hamstrings, and lateral gastrocnemius compared to walking forward lunges (WFL).
JFL requires a greater range of motion at the hip, knee, and ankle joints compared to WFL.
The altered kinematics of JFL result in longer rectus femoris and lateral hamstring muscle lengths during the movement.
Forward lunges do not primarily elicit eccentric hamstring activation as commonly believed; hamstrings contract eccentrically for only a small portion of the lunge cycle.
The rectus femoris and lateral gastrocnemius undergo significantly longer periods of eccentric contraction during both walking and jumping forward lunges.
specific_findings: Study population consisted of five athletes.
Hamstring muscle groups were active eccentrically during only 18% (WFL) and 19% (JFL) of the lunge cycles.
The rectus femoris muscle contracted eccentrically for 54% (WFL) and 44% (JFL) of the lunge cycle.
The lateral gastrocnemius muscle contracted eccentrically for 61% (WFL) and 63% (JFL) of the lunge cycle.
In the WFL, the second EMG burst of the rectus femoris begins at 20% stance and peaks at approximately 40% of the stance phase.
In the JFL, the second EMG burst of the rectus femoris begins at 20% stance and peaks at approximately 60% stance.

core_principles: During the initial phase of a forward lunge, negative work is performed to decelerate downward vertical momentum.
Hamstring length is determined by both knee and hip angles, with the hip angle having a greater impact due to a longer moment arm.
In a walking forward lunge, the rectus femoris elongates at foot strike and at the end of the movement to control the motion.
In a jumping forward lunge, the rectus femoris undergoes significant elongation and high activation at foot strike to absorb high impact forces.
The gastrocnemius undergoes prolonged eccentric contraction during the stance phase of both walking and jumping lunges to prepare for the concentric push-off.
specific_findings: Eccentric hamstring contraction accounts for 18% (WFL) and 19% (JFL) of the total lunge cycle from approach to toe-off.
The gastrocnemius exhibits a similar amount of eccentric contraction in both lunge motions: 61% in walking forward lunge and 63% in jumping forward lunge.
Quasi-isometric contraction with relatively high hamstring muscle activity occurs during the initial phases (approximately 0–20%) of the forward lunge.

core_principles: Progress from Walking Forward Lunges (WFL) to Jump Forward Lunges (JFL) to minimize injury risk due to the high activation levels of JFL.
Understand that the quadriceps contract eccentrically during the first part of a forward lunge, particularly during the JFL.
Note that the hamstrings perform an isometric contraction during the initial period of the stance phase, rather than a prolonged eccentric contraction.
The gastrocnemius works eccentrically during most of the stance phase of the lunge.
common_mistakes: Attempting high-intensity variations like the Jump Forward Lunge (JFL) before building sufficient strength and control with the Walking Forward Lunge (WFL).
specific_findings: The activation values during the lunges often exceeded 100% MVIC (maximum voluntary isometric contraction).
Contrary to popular belief in the track and field community, the forward lunge is not an exercise that elicits prolonged eccentric hamstring activity.
